title: Who is at the door?
hook: a lover knocks, says "it is I," and is sent away until he learns to answer "it is you" (Masnavi 1.3056ff)

segments.voice: Last week ended with Marcus saying: of course there are rude people. Your line was of course. Did the two words help? Day two hundred thirteen.

You knock on a door, and from inside someone calls: who is it? And you say, without thinking: it's me. As if that explains everything. As if me were the most obvious thing in the world. Couples do it on the phone. Kids do it at the front door. Me! We say it all day long: my plan, my turn, my way, my feelings about it. A new week starts today. It's called guests, and it's about who we let in. And it begins at a door, with one of Rumi's shortest and most famous stories. Today: who is at the door?
screen: `WHO IS IT? IT'S ME.` → `A WEEK OF GUESTS.` → `WHO IS AT THE DOOR?`

segments.voice: It's in Book One of the Masnavi. A man comes to the door of the one he loves and knocks. From inside, the beloved asks: who are you? He answers: it's I. And the beloved says: go away. This isn't the time. There's no place at a table like this for someone raw. Remember raw from the chickpea last week? Raw means not yet cooked, still hard, still full of himself. So the man goes away. For a whole year he travels, burning with the pain of separation, and in Rumi's words, the fire cooks him. Then he comes back. He paces around the house, afraid some careless word will slip out again. He knocks. And the voice inside asks: who is at the door? This time he says: it is you. You, who hold my heart. And the beloved says: since you are I, come in. There isn't room in this house for two I's. That's the whole story. It works on a few levels. On the surface, it's about love between people: real love has less me in it. But Rumi is talking about God. The seeker comes to the door full of himself, and the door stays shut. Only when the self has been cooked down, when he can say it is you, is there room. Sufis would say it isn't that he disappears. It's that his I no longer stands between. Most of us aren't there yet. But you can feel the difference between arriving with it's me and arriving with it's you, even at a kitchen table. Your line: it is you.
screen: `WHO ARE YOU? IT'S I.` · `A YEAR OF BURNING.` · `IT IS YOU. COME IN.` · then, large: `NO ROOM FOR TWO I'S.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one I go today. Settle, and notice how often the word I or me shows up in your thoughts, even now. I'm doing this right. I'm tired. Me, me. Each time you notice it, just let it soften, like the knock on a door. Rest in what's here without the name tag. If you pray, you can rest in God's presence without saying who you are. The bell holds the time.
Who is at the door? A lover says it's I and is turned away, then returns after a year and says it's you, and is let in. Today's word.
screen: `WHO IS AT THE DOOR? — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: it is you. Today, in one conversation, drop one I: ask a question instead of telling your story, or let someone else's plan win. Day two hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: In Sufi teaching, this story is often told to describe the lessening of the ego on the way to God, and many readers also take it as a picture of selfless love between people.
